video:video.video:title: ADP Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The quote-only posture is normal in payroll, so the honest complaint is not that ADP hides its price — it is what that does to you as a buyer. You cannot compare ADP against anyone without first giving a salesperson your headcount and your phone number. And the three-months-free banner carries an end date, which puts a clock on a decision you cannot yet cost. Ask for the per-employee-per-month rate and the per-payroll-run fee separately. Ask what you pay from month seven, since the offer terms credit the free months to months 4 to 6. And ask what the price becomes at double your current headcount, because payroll pricing steps rather than scales smoothly. One detail worth noticing: ADP does publish an /llms.txt, a file whose entire purpose is to guide AI assistants around its site. They are willing to machine-readably explain what they sell. They are not willing to say what it costs.

video:video.video:title: AccuWeb Hosting Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan prices are introductory rates on a 24-month term and renew at about two to four times as much: VPS Edge goes from €4.42 to €8.91 a month, VPS Power from €8.88 to €35.68. The money-back guarantee is 7 days, shorter than many hosts offer, and the prices shown change with your location and currency. The support response figures and customer numbers on the site are AccuWeb's own claims. We have not used AccuWeb Hosting ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Airia Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Airia used to publish part of its ladder, which was refreshingly rare for enterprise AI. As of 20 August 2026 that is over: the pricing page redirects into developer documentation on airia.ai from both airia.com and www.airia.com, and there is no amount anywhere on the site. So the honest position is now the usual one for this category — you cannot budget before a sales conversation. The underlying fit has not changed, though the pitch has. Read on 1 September 2026, the site leads with discovery and enforcement rather than building: finding the AI tools, models, agents and MCP servers already running, including the unapproved ones, stopping actions at the execution layer before the tool call fires, and mapping governance evidence to the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, SR 11-7, HIPAA, ISO 42001 and SOC 2. The agent builder now sits under Optimize. Either way this only pays off at organisational scale. A small team that wants one chatbot is buying far more platform than it needs. For an enterprise standardising and governing AI, that is exactly the point.

video:video.video:title: Aplos Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline you will see first is not the price you will pay. The 50%-off banner sits at the top of the page and rewrites every figure on it, so the $39.50 that catches your eye is a three-month rate against a $79 list price — a 100% increase waiting in month four, on software that holds your books and is therefore painful to leave. The second thing to pin down is what grows with you: each user beyond the two included adds $20 a month, every 1,000 contacts beyond 500 adds another $20, and on Lite every user is a full Administrator, because role permissions start at Core.

video:video.video:title: Arbor Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catches: it only exists in deregulated US states, and it only touches the supply rate, since delivery charges stay with your utility. The headline savings — Arbor itself reports an average of up to $593/year — depend entirely on how bad your current default rate is. If you already shopped your rate recently, the gain may be small.

video:video.video:title: Assembly Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two meters run at once. Active contacts bite first: Starter stops at 50, and the step to 500 costs $70 more a month on yearly billing ($90 monthly). Internal users are the other, and they get dearer as you climb: an extra colleague is $29 a month on Professional and $59 on Advanced (yearly-billed; $39 and $79 monthly), so the more expensive plan makes each additional person more expensive too. A newer third meter is build credits for the AI app builder — 200 a month on every paid plan, $0.60 each beyond that.

video:video.video:title: Atto Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Simple and honest pricing — the real conversation with any field-team tracker is the human one: GPS tracking of employees needs transparency and often consent (rules differ by country), and adoption dies the day the crew feels surveilled rather than served. Roll it out as 'accurate paychecks and fewer timesheet fights', involve the team, and the tool pays for itself; roll it out as surveillance and no feature list saves it.

video:video.video:title: BackupMaster Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The listing header says free to install, and there is a free tier, but it is not for you unless you are an agency: Agency is limited to Shopify Partner development stores before they are handed over to a client. For a live store the entry price is $19 a month and it buys 300 orders a month.
Restore is described on the listing as restoring supported items, and the list of what that excludes lives in the documentation rather than on the listing. It matters. Read on 10 October 2026, the coverage page says orders are backed up but cannot be restored or cloned, because Shopify limits updates to existing orders. Locations, saved searches, policies and shipping zones are backup-only, and inventory comes back only through a manual download and Shopify's own inventory import. Store settings, third-party app data, reviews, redirects, coupons, companies, catalogs and analytics are not covered at all. Read that page before you rely on the product, and run one real restore into a development store rather than discovering the boundary during an incident.
The most useful review on the page is the critical one. In April 2026 a merchant asked for exports over SFTP to storage the vendor does not control, on-demand backups before risky changes, configurable retention and languages beyond English and German. The same merchant noted that a second store costs extra here where some rivals include one. None of that is damning; it is a fair map of where this app currently stops. One of those requests has since been met in part: the documentation now describes a Backup Now button for a manual backup at any time (read 10 October 2026). Worth adding to the same note: your store data sits with a vendor in Australia, which belongs in your processing register whatever you decide.

video:video.video:title: Beautiful.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The smart-template engine is the feature and the fence: decks look polished with zero design skill precisely because the system constrains you, so pixel-perfect custom layouts and heavy brand exceptions fight the tool. And note the billing gap — $14.50/mo annual becomes $45 month-to-month, one of the steeper monthly premiums around. If your organisation lives in PowerPoint workflows, test the import/export round-trip before committing.

video:video.video:title: Bill.com Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Per-user pricing plus per-transaction fees means the real cost depends on team size and payment volume — it's built for finance teams with genuine AP workflows and is overkill if you pay a handful of bills a month.

video:video.video:title: BillingNow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing is genuinely refreshing — two plans, same features on both, unlimited users, no per-seat maths. The honest watch-out is the trial length rather than its terms: three days is short for migrating billing into a new tool, and the practical constraint is that there is no import path. The help centre documents CSV and Excel export but no import, so an existing client list has to be retyped — which is more than three days of work for anyone with a real book. It is also a young product from a small Geneva maker, so weigh ecosystem depth and longevity before you move your billing history in.

video:video.video:title: Bitvavo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest caveats are crypto-wide, not Bitvavo-specific: fees are only part of the cost (spread matters on small orders), and no exchange removes market risk — the platform being cheap and MiCA-regulated doesn't make the assets safe. Note the disclosure: this is one of the few tools here we genuinely run — our own trading system executes on Bitvavo — which is experience, but also means we're an actual customer, not a neutral bystander.

video:video.video:title: Bizee Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $0 headline leaves out the state filing fee, which is usually the larger part of the bill, and the package contents only show after you choose an entity and a state. The free registered agent year ends, and the standalone service is listed at $149 a year. Refunds stop once Bizee forwards your payment to the state, typically within 24 hours.

video:video.video:title: Blinq Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The core product is honestly cheap — the cost that grows hides in event lead capture, now billed per lead at $9.99 a credit on top of the Business seats (read 7 October 2026), which is where teams that live on trade shows actually get value. And a truth about all digital cards: the wow factor works precisely because adoption is still low; the durable value is the CRM sync (contacts flowing automatically into your pipeline), so judge Business tier by that integration, not by the tap-to-share trick.

video:video.video:title: Bokun Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Bokun is a Tripadvisor/Viator company, and that's both the draw and the lock-in. Distribution to Viator and 2,600+ resellers is excellent, but you're building your booking backbone inside one OTA's ecosystem, and the per-booking service fee on direct sales is a real cut on top of the subscription — although any paid plan lets you pass that fee to the guest instead of absorbing it. The zero-fee promise on Viator bookings has one exception the tier table does not show: Channel Manager customers pay 0.5-1.5% on Viator reservations. If most of your business is direct, weigh that fee; if you live on OTA distribution, the Viator advantage is hard to beat.

video:video.video:title: Bolt Business Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest boundary is geography: Bolt's network is Europe/Africa-centric across 600+ cities, so US-only operations should look elsewhere, and ride availability varies by city — pilot it on your team's actual routes. Pricing is dynamic like all ride-hailing; the business layer adds control and receipts, not fixed corporate fares, so budget-predictability comes from your spend limits, not from locked prices.

video:video.video:title: BookX Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan is a demonstration rather than a plan. One service and one team member means a salon with two stylists, or a studio running two class types, is already on Starter — so treat $9.99 a month as the real entry price, not zero. From there the ladder is gated on locations and team members rather than on how much you actually book: five, ten and twenty at $9.99, $19.99 and $39.99. A busy single-location business therefore pays the same as a quiet one, which is generous, while a small chain climbs the ladder for reasons that have nothing to do with volume. Above twenty locations or team members the published table stops and you have to ask. And the whole thing only exists inside Shopify — the calendar rides on your storefront, checkout and POS — so there is nothing here for a business that takes bookings anywhere else.

video:video.video:title: Bybit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Derivatives are the draw and the danger: leverage cuts both ways, and funding rates on perpetuals are a real recurring cost the fee table doesn't show. Regulation-wise, check what Bybit may offer in YOUR jurisdiction before funding an account — availability and product range differ per country, and that's the part most fee comparisons skip.

video:video.video:title: CO2 Impact Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every licence is a 12-month commitment, and on 9 October automated electricity and gas data was billed extra per meter per year; the redesigned pricing table of 22 October no longer shows add-on prices at all, so extra users, sites and meter feeds have to be quoted. The free trial is Basic only, for 7 days, with up to 10 entries per activity category and no reports, so you cannot test the output you are buying. We have not used CO2 Impact ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Carbon6 Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest headline here is not pricing but ownership — and it has moved again, this time in the reader's favour. SPS Commerce bought Carbon6 for roughly $210M on 7 Feb 2025 and retired the brand into spscommerce.com. On 30 Jun 2026 it sold the entire 3P (Amazon marketplace seller) revenue-recovery business for $9.5M cash, booking an estimated $20M loss, and named no buyer at the time. There is a name now. The partner-programme notice we received on 17 Aug 2026, from Carbon6's own partnerships contact, states that SPS transferred ownership of the 3P business to Carbon6 and that commission terms and payouts are unchanged. It also states that existing links were redirected to the Carbon6 tool sites on 14 Aug 2026, and that the programme itself rebrands from SPS to Carbon6 on 24 Aug 2026. Reading carbon6.io on 17 Aug 2026 matches that: the whole suite is on sale there again as "by Carbon6". Read the two purchase numbers carefully, because they are not the same thing. The $210M bought the whole Carbon6 stack; the $9.5M was the 3P arm alone, and offloading it at a book loss seventeen months in still tells you how it performed. What remains undisclosed is who stands behind the Carbon6 entity itself, so the question is answered one level down and no further. Two more things to hold. Reuters reported on 23 Jun 2026 that SPS hired Morgan Stanley to explore a sale of itself under activist pressure, with talks early and no deal assured. And the 1P side is no longer a clean split, because SPS kept the deduction-recovery business it bought while Carbon6's own site now lists ChargeGuard for Amazon 1P vendor recovery. Ask which entity your 1P work would sit with before you sign. For 3P reimbursements the July advice has expired — you can name the counterparty on your contract again.

video:video.video:title: Checkr Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline per-check price is rarely what you actually pay — passthrough fees vary wildly by county and search type, so budget for the effective cost, not the advertised one. It's overkill unless you hire at real volume.

video:video.video:title: ChemiCloud Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is the one every budget host shares: the headline price is an introductory rate, and renewals land roughly three times higher, so judge it on the renewal cost, not the sign-up teaser. Support and performance reviews are genuinely strong for the price band, but this is shared/managed hosting — if you need serious dedicated resources or enterprise SLAs, you'll outgrow the cheap tiers. Great value to start, just enter with eyes open on renewal.

video:video.video:title: Claude Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is usage limits: even on Pro you can hit a ceiling mid-session on a heavy day, and the step up to Max is a real $100 to $200 a month — you're buying headroom, not extra features. It also doesn't generate images, so if that's your main need it's the wrong tool, and its third-party plugin ecosystem is smaller than ChatGPT's.

video:video.video:title: CloudTask Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $299 is the honest part and also the small part: their FAQ calls it a one-time deposit to start a search, denies any monthly platform fee, and says it goes toward your first placement. What you will actually spend is the all-in monthly rate per hire, and that figure appears nowhere on the pricing page — you get it after you talk to them, once you are already invested in the process. Work out before you start what a comparable LATAM salary is on your own, so you can see what the managed layer costs on top. The exit is worth reading twice too. You can convert a managed hire onto your own payroll, but CloudTask's FAQ attaches a conversion fee and a notice period to that and publishes neither. So the price of keeping the person is a number you cannot check in advance.

video:video.video:title: Compliancely Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing page prices one product and the marketing sells about a dozen. Every tier you can actually buy online is an allowance of TIN verifications. The moment you want the things the homepage leads with — KYB business verification, credit-risk assessment, address verification, Form I-9 and E-Verify, IRS tax transcripts, OFAC and watchlist monitoring — the button changes from Get Started to Contact Sales. So the compliance stack this tool is pitched as has no advertised cost, and the number you can see is the smallest part of it. The second thing to read carefully is that the tiers are allowances rather than rates. You commit to a monthly verification count up front, and the per-match price moves against the smallest buyers. It is $0.79 a check on the cheapest month-to-month plan versus $0.54 on the largest annual one — a 46% spread that falls the wrong way for anyone testing the product at low volume. If your usage is lumpy — a filing-season spike and eleven quiet months — an allowance you buy every month is the wrong shape, and the Prepaid toggle is the shape to check first: it sells yearly packs from 50 verifications for $43.95 to 3,000 for $1,799.95 (read 12 October 2026), although on the small packs the price per match is higher than on the monthly subscriptions.

video:video.video:title: Contractor Foreman Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credit where it is due first: this is company pricing with unlimited projects and no per-user overage inside your tier, which is rare in construction software and genuinely cheaper than per-seat rivals for a crew. The catch is the billing term. Monthly costs 20% to 32% more than annual on the same plan — $139 against $105 on Standard — and Basic is sold on annual billing only, so the cheapest way in requires a year paid up front. The user counts are the real ladder: 1, 3, 8, 15, unlimited. A five-person crew is not on Standard at $105, it is on Plus at $166, so count your licence holders before you compare against anything else.

video:video.video:title: Credit Repair Cloud Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is business-in-a-box software for starting a credit-repair company, not a tool that repairs your own credit — the price only makes sense if you're actually building a client business on it. The middle tiers jump fast as you add clients and seats, and success depends far more on your sales and compliance discipline (credit repair is a regulated space) than on the software. Buy it as an operator, not a consumer.

video:video.video:title: Database Mart Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Database Mart is cheap partly because the hardware is older. Most GPU and dedicated rows pair the card with Xeon E3 and E5 processors, and even the $2,099-a-month H100 server lists two E5-2697v4 CPUs from 2016 and a 100Mbps port, which is slow for moving model weights or datasets. Every server is in Dallas, Texas, so there is no second region for European or Asian users. Many rows carry 26% to 54% discounts, which makes the table hard to compare: some smaller plans cost more than larger ones. The trust signals on the home page, 500K+ customers and 21 years in business, are the company's own and we could not check them, and we found no independent benchmark. Some dedicated and GPU builds may add a one-time provisioning fee that the table does not show.

video:video.video:title: Datarails Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You cannot find out what it costs without talking to sales, and the entry plan is smaller than it looks: Professional covers 2 users and 1 integration, so a finance team of three, or one that needs both the ERP and the CRM connected, is priced into the next tier before the conversation starts. There is no free plan, no free trial and no self-serve signup anywhere on the site — every path ends at Request Demo — so there is no way to try it quietly before procurement is involved.

video:video.video:title: Deel Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every price is a ‘starting at’ and every button says ‘book a demo’ — the real bill depends on countries, benefits and add-ons, and only firms up in a sales conversation. And know what EOR money buys: at $599+/month per employee you’re paying for compliance risk transfer, not software — worth it in unfamiliar jurisdictions, expensive where you could open your own entity.

video:video.video:title: Devs.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat price is the smaller half of the bill. Personal includes $10 of usage a month and Business $21, with model usage metered on top of the seat. The plan cards state the included amount without stating the rate you pay once it runs out — which is exactly the number you need to forecast a real workload. The free plan is a demo rather than a working tier: both builders are limited to "Core", and workflows, APIs and integrations are absent entirely, which is much of what would make the platform useful past a first agent. And for a product sold on IT governance, the governance controls are the ones you cannot buy with a card — SSO, access control lists and white-labelling sit on the Enterprise tier, behind a custom annual contract.

video:video.video:title: Dify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Free' self-hosting isn't free — you own the servers, updates and reliability, and model usage bills separately once the included message credits run out. Dify Cloud takes that infrastructure work off your hands, but every cloud plan is a single workspace, and multiple workspaces, SSO and a commercial licence sit in quote-only Enterprise. It's powerful, but self-hosting it well needs technical comfort.

video:video.video:title: Digit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tier price is a floor, not a ceiling, and the add-ons are where an inventory system quietly doubles. Two integrations are included — but a working setup usually means an accounting package and a webshop, which is your two, and then Amazon or a second sales channel is another $125 a month by the FAQ (the integrations block on the same page still says $100; we have asked which one bills). Want the API, or your data inside an AI assistant? $125 a month each. A Starter customer on QuickBooks, Shopify and Amazon with API access is at $650 a month on the FAQ's numbers, $625 on the block's, before adding a sixth user. Price the whole configuration you actually need, not the tier.

video:video.video:title: Disputifier Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Free to install is doing a lot of work here. All four services bill per event — a fifth of each recovery, $17 to $27.50 an alert, five cents an order twice over — so the cost lands after the fact and scales with exactly the thing you are trying to reduce. Model your worst chargeback month before you switch alerts on, not your average one.
The reviews deserve a straight look too. The 4.6 average across 125 reviews, read again on 17 September 2026, is not a middle: 87% are five stars and twelve of the one hundred and twenty-five are a single star, with almost nothing in between. That shape has held while the count grew — on 22 August the same listing showed 4.6 from 88 reviews with nine one-stars, so both ends have filled at roughly the same rate. The most recent one-star we read, from June 2026, describes a security incident at the vendor and a dispute over unpaid invoices and billing descriptors; Disputifier replied in July that it does not block merchants from moving providers and disputes the account of the charges. We have not verified either side and are not taking one. What the pattern does show is where the friction sits: merchants either rate this perfect or fall out with it over invoices, not over whether disputes were won.
And know what alerts cannot reach. Coverage depends on the shopper's bank and card: smaller issuers do not participate, Amex and Discover frequently cannot be set up, Klarna alerts do not exist yet and PayPal alerts are recent. The prevention rate the vendor quotes is a ceiling for a well-covered card mix, not a promise for yours.

video:video.video:title: DocSend Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The cheap plan is not the product people buy DocSend for. Personal at $10 a month tracks who opened a single document and for how long, but it has no data rooms at all. Sharing several files behind one link starts on Standard at $45 per user a month, and the controls that make a data room safe for a fundraise or a sale (visitor email authentication, watermarking, NDA gating, folder permissions) start on Advanced at $150 a month. Price the plan for the job you actually have, not the entry price on the page.
Monthly billing is expensive. The same Advanced plan costs $250 a month without a yearly commitment, two-thirds more than the $150 yearly rate, and Advanced Data Rooms goes from $180 to $300. A company that needs a data room for one four-month deal pays $1,000 on monthly billing, against $1,800 for a year it may not use. Work out that sum before you pick a toggle.
Several things a larger team will want are priced only through sales: the Salesforce integration, single sign-on and sub-teams. The trial is 14 days of the top plan, but visitors are capped during it, so a trial is not the place to run the real fundraise. We have not used DocSend ourselves; the figures here come from its pricing page and plan tooltips.

video:video.video:title: Dryground AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is consulting, not a tool you log into: best when you want AI designed and built for you, not when you'd rather DIY with software. Read the headline numbers carefully too. The 20-50% efficiency and 10-20% revenue figures on their homepage carry the caption “2025 industry benchmarks”, so they describe the market rather than this firm's own results. And the case studies underneath them name no clients.

video:video.video:title: Emergent Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The real cost is credit consumption, not the flat sticker -- Emergent's own guide says one prompt can cost from a handful of credits for a small UI tweak to hundreds for a full feature with tests, and a published app keeps drawing credits every month for its hosting tier, so serious builders run through a plan faster than the price list implies. Now do the division, because Emergent's own pricing page doesn't. Standard is $20 for 100 credits, so 20 cents a credit. Pro is $200 for 750, which is 26.7 cents. Moving up a tier makes every unit of work more expensive, not less: Pro costs 33% more per credit than Standard, and annual billing keeps the gap (17 cents against 22.3). That is the opposite of the volume discount the ladder looks like -- you are buying a 1M-token context window, custom agents and priority support, not cheaper work. Above Pro there is no bigger self-serve plan: Business and Enterprise are both quote-only. Top-up packs fill the gap at the Standard rate, 250 credits for $50 or 20 cents a credit, but they are non-refundable. Check what your month actually needs before you upgrade; one Standard month plus purchased extra credits may beat one Pro month. AI-generated code still needs a human eye: review it for security, correctness and maintainability before anything touches real users.

video:video.video:title: Employment Hero Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: There is no such thing as the Employment Hero price, and the first thing to fix is the currency: the pricing page is the Australian one, its disclaimer says every figure is AUD excluding GST, and there is no US page. Then the structure. HR, recruitment, chat and payroll are separate subscriptions, most of them per employee, with a stated minimum of ten users underneath — so a six-person company is billed for ten. Payroll no longer carries its own price at all: it is inside the quote-only Employment Unlimited tier, or an A$20-a-head add-on with a A$400 floor. And the recruitment tiers meter AI video interviews rather than people, with credits that reset monthly, do not roll over, and overage billed automatically with no hard cap.

video:video.video:title: ExpertEx Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan cards and the calculator on the same page do not agree, and the gap is large enough to pick the wrong tier. Starter is sold as 65 product photos and 10 short video ads a month on 1,000 credits; at the calculator's own rates that work costs 4,125 credits, four times the allowance. The card numbers only reconcile if each is taken alone, and at roughly 15 credits a photo and 100 a video. The same 4.2x mismatch repeats on every tier, so it is a systematic difference rather than a typo. Ask which rate governs before you buy, because the calculator will steer you to a plan two rungs above what the card implies. The second thing to price is that this is a credit product with no free tier. Prompt Builder is free; generating is not. And the cheap trials ($1, $2, $5) are three days rather than a month -- enough to test output quality, not enough to test a monthly workflow. And the fundamental one: AI product photography is judged on whether the output is publishable without a retoucher. Run your own worst product through the trial -- a reflective bottle, a garment with fine texture -- rather than the kind of thing that looks good in every demo.

video:video.video:title: Expertise AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is that you can no longer see what this costs. On 3 September 2026 the page still had a ladder: a Free Preview capped at 10 conversations, then Business at $2,000/mo, the $500 Growth tier having been withdrawn in August. By 1 October every amount was gone, the free preview with it, and all three tiers now end in 'Book a demo'. So the price is whatever the call produces, and the only public yardstick is the old $2,000 a month. It's also a RAG agent, so it's only as good as the docs you feed it: give it thin content and it can answer buyers confidently but wrong. Strong for HubSpot-centric B2B teams that are ready to buy through sales; hard to evaluate on your own.

video:video.video:title: Finale Inventory Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's built for real warehouse volume and priced that way: Essentials starts at $499 a month and Growth at $799, with Enterprise quoted. There is no self-serve tier and no published order or user cap -- every plan goes through Request a Demo, most customers sign 12- to 36-month terms, and API and EDI access are Enterprise-only. If you do a few dozen orders a month, this is far more inventory engine, and far more cost, than the job needs.

video:video.video:title: Flatpay Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: “Zero monthly fees” is the headline, and there genuinely is no subscription — but there is a floor. Miss £1,100 of card turnover in a month (the price list's figure on 14 October 2026, incl. VAT; it was £995 in September) and you are charged £39, which for a quiet month is the same thing as a monthly fee wearing a different hat. Do the sum before you sign: a shop turning over £500 on cards pays £7.45 in transaction fees and then £39 on top, so the cost of taking cards is six times what the rate suggests. The rate itself is straightforward and the terminal really is free to start, so this is a good fit for a busy till and a poor one for a market stall, a seasonal business or anyone whose card volume swings. And the four-figure POS installation charges are real money that the “no hidden fees” promise sits directly above — they are disclosed, but they are not what most people picture when they read that line.

video:video.video:title: FlexiQuiz Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The monthly response caps are the business model: 20 on free, 500 on Essentials, 2,000 on Premium and 25,000 on Enterprise -- one viral quiz or one big exam cohort and you're shopping a tier up. The cap hits the participant, not you: in our test on 20 October 2026 the 21st respondent of the month saw only 'This account has reached the maximum monthly response limit' instead of the quiz. The free plan also stops at 10 questions, a limit that only shows up when you save the eleventh. The per-response price falls steeply as you climb ($0.034, $0.0125, $0.0024 on yearly billing), so the ceiling is the thing to price, not the sticker. Administrator seats are capped separately at 1, 2 and 15, and sharing a login is against the terms.

video:video.video:title: Foxit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Foxit's pitch is being the honest fraction of Acrobat's price, and on the headline numbers it delivers. The catch used to be that e-signing was always a second subscription. As of our 28 August 2026 reading that is only true below Editor+, which now includes Foxit eSign with 150 envelopes a year. The trap has moved rather than gone: buy the $129.99 Editor, then find you need signatures, and Editor plus standalone eSign Essentials is $249.99 a year against $159.99 for the Editor+ that bundles it. AI is still an add-on at $49.99 a year beyond the 300 monthly credits, and it is not sold for perpetual licences at all. Price the basket, not the first line.

video:video.video:title: FreshBooks Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things multiply the number you first see. The promotional rates end: Lite is $1 a month for the first year and $23 after that, and Plus and Premium are 80% off for three months only. And the meter is billable clients, not invoices or revenue: Lite stops at five, which a freelancer with a handful of retainers passes in their first good quarter, and the step to fifty clients is $43. Then people cost extra on top at $11 each, so a two-person studio on Plus is $54 a month rather than $43. Payroll is a separate $40 plus $6 a head, which is the line most people miss when they compare this against a bookkeeping tool that includes it.

video:video.video:title: Freshservice Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $19 headline rarely survives contact with a real deployment: the ITSM features most IT teams buy for (change/problem management, deeper analytics) live at Pro, and so does Freddy AI Copilot, a $29-an-agent add-on offered only on Pro and Enterprise. Orchestration runs and, from Growth up, 100 asset units come included; you pay extra only past those allowances. Price the tier that contains your must-haves plus the add-ons you would switch on, not the starter row. Within that honesty, it's one of the fastest ITSM tools to actually stand up.

video:video.video:title: GCheck Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The pricing page reads like self-serve and is not. “Pay per screen” sits above three published prices, but every Get Started with Basic, Standard or Advanced button on that page opens the same contact form as Book a Demo, asking for your company name. There is no checkout: an employer who wants to run one check this afternoon starts with a sales conversation, and the price you are quoted after it is the one to hold them to.
The $18.95 check is narrower than the headline suggests. Basic searches county court records only in the candidate's current county of residence, and GCheck's own FAQ calls the county search the gold standard for criminal record accuracy while describing the national database search as covering participating jurisdictions. A candidate who moved last year has their previous counties searched only from Standard at $39.95, which is the package GCheck itself marks Most Popular. Then there is the asterisk under every price: third-party fees may apply to some products and are passed through with no markup, and nothing on the site says which products or how much. County court access fees are the usual example in this industry, so budget for the package price plus fees you will see for the first time on an invoice.
The rest of the catalogue is unpriced. Drug tests, driving records, employment and education verification, credit and civil searches, fingerprinting and international searches are all listed and none carries a figure, so a role that needs an MVR or an employment verification on top of the criminal search is a quote, not a sum. The same goes for integrations: GCheck's integrations page names 18 ATS and HRIS systems, including Greenhouse, Lever, Workday, BambooHR and Rippling, but the pricing page places integrations under the custom quote for employers running more than 50 checks a year, and its FAQ sends you to sales for the list.
On track record we can tell you less than we would like. The 12–24 hour average turnaround and same-day results

video:video.video:title: Glide Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Glide meters updates, not just seats. Your bill tracks how busy the app is rather than how many people own a licence. A write-heavy workflow can pass the included 5,000 updates and add 2 cents each without anyone changing plan. The jump from Maker to Business is also steep: $49 to $199 per month on annual billing, and the row ceiling only moves from 25k to 100k. Per Glide's partner team on 18 August 2026, those ceilings track the data source rather than the plan. 25k applies to synced spreadsheet sources whatever you pay, and the 100k+ figures belong to their Big Table source. So an upgrade alone does not lift a spreadsheet-backed app past 25k rows. The pricing page is hard to read for a reason Glide does not dispute. Asked about the Individual and Business tabs, the same team called them audience segmentation. They agreed on 18 August 2026 that the comparison tables confuse, because they never put all plans side by side. And there is a trap before any of that arithmetic applies: everything above describes the classic builder, but the free signup button on glideapps.com does not lead there. We pressed it on 7 September 2026 and landed in GlideOS, the newer AI product, which meters credits instead of updates, starts at $25 a month instead of $199, and describes its free tier only as “limited credits” with no number anywhere in the pricing page or the app. Read the classic prices, click sign up, and you are evaluating something else.

video:video.video:title: Gravity Forms Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest notes. It's a WordPress-only plugin — no WordPress, no Gravity Forms — and its real power often lives in paid add-ons and third-party extensions, so a genuinely advanced setup can cost more than the base license suggests. It's developer-friendly rather than beginner-slick; non-technical users may find hosted builders more polished. For a WordPress site, though, it's the reliable gold standard.

video:video.video:title: Guesty Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pricing runs higher than leaner rivals, onboarding has a learning curve, and some users flag support — it earns its keep at scale, but it's heavy for a single listing.

video:video.video:title: Gusto Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The base-plus-per-employee model is transparent but adds up, and Gusto is US-only — excellent for straightforward US payroll and benefits, but not the pick for international teams or complex multi-entity HR.

video:video.video:title: Harbor Compliance Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The $99 on every page is a first-year price. Registered agent renews at $159 a year, about 60% more, and the only way to keep $99 is to prepay two or three years. The same page sets its own price against an unnamed 'competition' at $250 to $350 'with large annual increases', which is a comparison you cannot check, and its own renewal is an increase too. Budget on $159.
The recurring filing is where the bill grows. Annual report service is $199 per state per year, plus the state's own fee, which Harbor invoices before the due date. For a company registered in three states that is $597 a year in service fees before any state charges, on top of a registered agent in each of those states. Volume discounts of up to 40% exist, but only online and without a published table.
The formation price is a starting point rather than a package. LLC formation and incorporation both read 'starting at $99 plus state fees', and the public pages do not list what the $99 covers or what the higher options add; the answer is in the order flow. The software that the agent service leans on, Entity Manager, is included with the agent, but the wider software suite has no published price and starts with a demo.
The ratings on the pages are Google reviews that Harbor Compliance quotes itself. We found no independent reviews we could read for this dossier, and we have not used the service.

video:video.video:title: Heard Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Mind the fine print between tiers: the entry plan does not include your annual tax filing (a $750 add-on on Lite), month-to-month billing costs $20 to $50 a month more than the annual rate, and messy back-months cost extra as catch-up fees. Price the tier that actually includes filing.

video:video.video:title: Hive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat price is honest bait, the add-on grid is the business model: switch on three add-ons and your $12 seat becomes $27 — a la carte flexibility that punishes teams who need the full toolkit. List your must-have modules first and compare the DRESSED price against all-inclusive rivals; for teams needing only core PM, though, Hive is genuinely cheap and pleasant. In our test on 21 October 2026 two defaults stood out: onboarding lets everyone on your email domain join the workspace automatically unless you untick it, and completed tasks disappear from the List view behind a filter.

video:video.video:title: Hopp Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest note is that the platform is free and the rides are not. Hopp Business charges no activation fee and no minimum commitment, so the whole cost is ride pricing, which moves with city, vehicle class and demand — and coverage thins out wherever Bolt does not already run. Check both on your own routes before you move a travel budget across.

video:video.video:title: HostPapa Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $2.95 is a first-term price on a 3-year term for new customers only, and the regular rate is three to four times higher: Essentials renews at $8.99 a month on a 3-year term and $12.99 month to month. Essentials hosts one site. Automated backups and the domain are free for the first year only, and cancelling inside the first term costs a non-refundable domain fee whose amount the page does not state. The home page puts VPS hosting at $2.95 a month while the web-hosting page says VPS starts at $19.99, so read the VPS page itself before you plan on it. Prices exclude taxes. The support and customer figures on the site are HostPapa's own claims, and we have not used HostPapa ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Hostinger Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline price only holds if you prepay years up front — renewals run several times the intro rate, the number-one complaint. Budget for the renewal, and be realistic that budget shared hosting isn't managed-grade performance.

video:video.video:title: Housecall Pro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The Basic tier is a trap for real field teams — it omits GPS tracking and QuickBooks sync, so most businesses need Essentials or up. And the seats are the expensive part: users beyond the eight on MAX cost $35 a month each, and the page no longer states the extra-seat price on Essentials, on top of card processing quoted as 'as low as' 2.59% and a 1% fee on bank payments. Price the tier and the headcount you'll actually need.

video:video.video:title: Hubstaff Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat definition is the whole story and they state it plainly, which deserves credit: you pay for every seat you have created, not every person actually being tracked. So an account that grew with your headcount and never got tidied up is billing you for people who left. Audit your seat list before renewal, not after. The second thing is that features on the lower tiers are add-ons rather than inclusions — Insights, Tasks, Silent app and extra screenshots at $2.50 a seat a month, Locations at $3.33 — so the plan you priced and the plan that does what you watched in the demo may differ by ten dollars a seat. And be clear with yourself about why you are buying it: screenshots and activity levels change how a team feels about their work, and that cost does not appear on any pricing page.

video:video.video:title: IDrive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The first-year price is a teaser and the renewal is the price — IDrive says so itself under the plan table, and on the current numbers the step from discounted to standard is about 43% (Personal 5 TB goes from $6.99 to $9.99 a month). Budget on year-two rates, not the banner, and note that the discount is for new signups only and not available through their mobile apps. Overrun your storage and there is a further $0.25/GB/month on Personal, $0.50 on Team and Business. Beyond that, the honest backup fundamentals apply: a backup you never test-restore is a hope, not a backup, and the first full backup of multi-TB data takes weeks over the wire unless you use their physical Express seed shipping.

video:video.video:title: InVideo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is the credit model — each plan is a fixed monthly credit allowance that different models consume at different rates, and unused credits do not roll over, so a heavy month can exhaust an allowance long before it renews while a slow month simply wastes what you paid for. There is also no free way in any more: on 31 August 2026 the pricing page published no free tier at all, and on 24 September 2026 the cheapest route to trying it was Starter at $20 a seat a month, with 400 credits. AI video is fast but generic by default: templated output needs real editing and brand direction to not look like everyone else's. Treat it as a first-draft engine, not a finished-studio replacement.

video:video.video:title: Inbox Zero Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: There is no free plan: the trial needs a card and converts unless you cancel, though the site leads with 'Get started free'. Pricing is per user, and a second mailbox needs Plus. The terms of service date from July 2023, are short, name no company and say nothing about refunds; the refund promise lives only in the pricing FAQ, within 14 days of upgrading and at the vendor's judgement of value. The service reads your whole mailbox and passes email content to third-party AI providers. Security and popularity claims (SOC 2 Type 2, GitHub stars) are the vendor's own. We have not used Inbox Zero ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Jane Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Work out your price from your practitioner count, not from the plan headline. Practice at $79 covers one full-time practitioner; every other person who takes bookings adds $35 a month, or $17.50 if they book fewer than 24 hours a week. A clinic with three full-time practitioners pays $79 + 2 x $35 = $149 a month on Practice, and $99 + 2 x $40 = $179 on Thrive. Front-desk staff without bookable hours are free, which is generous, but a part-timer who creeps past 24 booked hours a week moves to the full-time rate.
The $59 Balance plan is for one practitioner seeing fewer than 20 clients a month. The limit counts invoices, so it is reached quickly, and it is also the plan Jane suggests you drop to if you leave and still need access to your records.
Insurance billing is an account-wide add-on, not a per-person one: $20 a month plus $5 for every extra full-time practitioner, whether or not they bill insurance, and in the US you still need your own Claim.MD clearinghouse account. There is no free trial: you get a demo call, or a shared demo account whose login the vendor hands out weekly through its community or support team.
Check the region. Jane is a Canadian company and several things on its Canadian page, such as Jane Payroll and direct insurance billing with Canadian insurers, are not on the US page, while UK prices are much lower than US ones. We have not used Jane; this review is based on the vendor's pricing page and FAQ in three regions.

video:video.video:title: Jibble Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Free forever with unlimited users holds up: the plan a new account lands on is Free, €0, with no card. What free leaves out is now readable too, because Jibble's own plan comparison sits inside the app even though the public pricing page is gone. The biggest gaps for a payroll process are timesheet approvals, automatic break deductions and more than one admin; our hands-on test below lists everything Free leaves out and keeps.
Two things to know before you build a process on it. A new organisation starts with a 14-day trial of the paid features, so for the first two weeks nothing looks locked; the limits above only show from day 15. Set up your workflow on what Free keeps, not on what week one showed you. And the paid tiers are cheap per head but add up: timesheet approvals and groups start at €1.79 per user a month on annual billing, €2.99 if you pay monthly, so a team of 25 pays €537 a year for the step most payroll processes need first.

video:video.video:title: Jubilee Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a focused vertical tool — bankruptcy petition preparation and case management — so its whole value is bounded by that practice area; a general legal practice won't get much from it. The case-count tiers are the thing to size correctly: pick 36 vs 300 by your real annual filing volume, and check whether the pay-per-case option is cheaper if you file sporadically. For a bankruptcy practice, the automation and court-form handling are exactly the point.

video:video.video:title: Krystal Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Krystal does not win on sticker price. Shown before VAT, Amethyst is £8.40 a month for a UK buyer and holds one site on 10GB, while budget hosts lead with multi-year introductory rates far below that (which then renew higher). 'Unlimited' from Emerald up is bounded by a 2,500,000-inode limit and 75 to 150 processes, round-the-clock phone support starts only at Sapphire (£37), changing your billing cycle takes a support ticket, and VPS is billed monthly only. Cancelling immediately schedules your sites and email for deletion within hours. We have not run Krystal ourselves; this dossier is read from Krystal's own pages and help centre, and we found no independent test we could weigh.

video:video.video:title: Leavo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tidy per-user numbers are annual-billed, and it's priced per seat — every employee you track adds to the bill, with no volume break published (large teams are told to ask sales). And the “free” is a 30-day trial, not a permanent free tier: budget for the paid plan from day 31.

video:video.video:title: Liltio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It runs only on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15.5 or later, so Windows users and owners of Intel Macs are out, and one licence covers 2 Macs. Speech recognition is local, but if you switch on a configured remote AI for text transforms, your prompts, text and relevant context go to that provider. We found no refund terms on the pricing page.

video:video.video:title: Melio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan is genuinely useful for low bill volume, but the value case narrows as you scale into paid tiers — and the 2.9% card fee only makes sense when you're deliberately floating cash on a card for rewards or timing.

video:video.video:title: Mera Work Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The price is low and the feature list is long; the catch sits in the data rather than the bill. Mera Work keeps your records for 90 days. The pricing table says data retention up to three months, and the privacy policy spells it out: unless your order form says otherwise, customer data is held on a rolling 90-day basis and anything older may be deleted automatically from production. That rules it out as the place you look back from over a year: an annual review, a client disputing hours billed last spring, a payroll audit. Export the timesheets and attendance you need every month, or get a longer retention period written into the order form before you roll it out.
This is monitoring software, not only a timer. The feature table lists screenshots, live screen streaming, keyboard and mouse activity tracking and a stealth mode. Mera Work's own pages are more careful than the word keystroke suggests: its keystroke feature records how much typing happened and when, not the keys or words themselves, and screenshots can be blurred and limited by role. But whether you may run screenshots, live view or a hidden agent on your staff's computers is a question for your employment adviser, not the vendor, and data-protection rules in Europe generally expect employees to be told what is recorded. Decide the policy first and tell people what the agent captures.
Two practical points. The company behind it, Aapna Infotheek Private Limited, is based in New Delhi, and its privacy policy says data may be hosted or processed in India; if you need it kept elsewhere, ask about the private cloud configuration the feature table lists and put it in the contract. And the review sites we normally read, Capterra and G2, blocked our reader on 30 September 2026. The one we could read, SoftwareSuggest, shows six reviews from 2025 under the old name Mera Monitor, and one of the three visible there also runs as a testimonial on Mera Work's own pricing page, so we found no clearly independent accoun

video:video.video:title: MigrationPro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Start with what is no longer there. Read on 5 October 2026, the Shopify App Store listing says the app is not currently available and sends support questions to the vendor: no install button, no review page. The vendor's site is still live and still selling, and every install button on its homepage and pricing page still points at that listing, so ask them how you install before you plan a migration date around it.
When the listing was up it told you nothing about what this costs: “Free to install. Additional charges may apply”, and a single plan block saying pricing is tailored to the entities you migrate. The number lives on the vendor's calculator, and the first number you find there — $29 — is the floor for the smallest store on the self-service route, not the price for yours. Their own homepage says a typical store lands between $49 and $299. Run the calculator before you form an opinion about value.
The add-on structure used to be the unknowable part, and as of 18 September 2026 it is not: the pricing page lists every add-on with a price, from $19 to $39, and marks all of them included on the managed plan. That is a real improvement in what a buyer can read before committing. It also makes the self-service route look less like $29 — the 301 redirects add-on, which is the one thing a migrating store can least afford to get wrong, is a $29 extra on a $29 migration.
The marketing still runs ahead of the evidence. The pricing page says “Trusted by 250,000+ stores”, the homepage uses the same figure for migrations, and the FAQ says 250,000+ migrations over 13 years — one number doing three different jobs. The same page, and an FAQ answer saying the app is available on the Shopify App Store, still claim 5.0 from 170+ verified reviews, which nobody can check while the listing is down. On 18 September it showed 186, of which 181 were five-star, 4 four-star and one a single star. Those reviews were genuinely good; weigh them rather than the banner.
One practical li

video:video.video:title: MindStudio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The no-markup model pass-through is genuinely fair — but it also means your real cost is subscription PLUS model spend, and an agent that loops or processes big documents burns provider credits invisibly until you set limits. The honest build discipline: start every agent with usage caps, and treat 'no-code' as no-code for the plumbing — the logic design and prompt quality are still entirely on you.

video:video.video:title: Miro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Per-member pricing charges for every member added to the workspace, so an org-wide rollout multiplies at full headcount — and the free plan's cap of 3 editable boards is workspace-wide, not per person. In our test on 20 October 2026 Miro did not block a fourth board: it warned that the oldest board would become view-only, and a new free team already starts with one board made for you. Model who truly needs to edit before you buy seats.

video:video.video:title: Modge Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The numbers on Modge's own pages do not agree with each other. The homepage says trusted by 1,000+ teams, the affiliate page says 1,800+ teams, the pricing page says over 2,000 users; the pricing page also shows three star ratings, 4.6 from 1,500 reviews, 4.8 from 2,000 and 4.2 from 800, without naming a single platform they come from. None of that touches the product, but it is the kind of copy a buyer should not repeat in a business case. What does touch the product is the comparison table: SSO through SAML 2.0, SOC 2 Type II and ISO 9001 are all marked soon, and HIPAA compliant appears with no report behind it. If your security review needs a document today, there is none to hand over. The desktop agent is macOS and Windows only, and the pricing page mentions no mobile app or GPS, so field teams are out of scope.

video:video.video:title: Momence Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Momence stopped publishing prices in September 2026: on the 25th its pricing page was a 'Let's talk pricing' form with no figure on it. The last public ladder (6 September) made the 'free' plan the most expensive one at real volume — 5% of every sale overtook Pro's $60 flat fee around $29k a year, and Pro lost to the $199 Custom plan above about $67k — while Pro added no features over Basic. Ask whether your quote is a flat fee or a percentage before you ask anything else.

video:video.video:title: Mycroft Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing page is a feature list with the prices taken out, and that is a choice rather than an oversight — Mycroft publishes what is in each package down to the individual capability, then stops short of the one line you came for. It matters more here than it would elsewhere, because what Mycroft sells is not a seat of software: it is a platform bundled with a managed service, secure enclaves, infrastructure and identity management, an audit coordinated on your behalf and, at the top, a dedicated CISO. That is a services contract, and services contracts scope on your environment, so the number genuinely will differ per company. It also means you cannot sanity-check the cost against doing it yourself until you have sat through a demo. The second thing to weigh is how much of the evidence is the vendor talking. What you can verify from outside is a handful of named case studies — SmashSend, Weave, Wisedocs, Unified — and the quotes inside them; there is no published customer count and no independent review base to read. The team is not thin: the CEO holds a CISA, the engineering co-founder a CISSP, and the product co-founder co-founded PartnerStack. But a young company promising CMMC and FedRAMP outcomes is asking for trust on a timeline where being wrong is expensive. Ask what happens if the assessment does not pass, and ask it before the second call.

video:video.video:title: Navan Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Free' is real but has a mechanism: Navan earns commission on bookings made through its inventory, so the platform's incentive is that your travel flows through Navan, and pricing on specific routes/hotels deserves an occasional spot-check against direct booking. The free Business plan stops at 300 employees and lists corporate negotiated rates as an Enterprise feature; expense management is free for 5 users and $15 per user per month after that.

video:video.video:title: Ngram Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The sticker price buys a credit allowance, not finished video, and the two are easy to confuse. Premium AI generation runs from 10 credits a second, so Basic's 3,000 credits a month come out at roughly 300 seconds — about five minutes of generated footage. Ngram says as much on the page: generation seconds measure premium AI-generated footage, not final video length, and manual editing and exports are unlimited on paid plans. So the tier you need tracks how much AI footage you generate, not how many videos you publish.
The top-up economics run the wrong way for small buyers. Extra credits cost 1,000 for $40 on Free, $20 on Basic, $15 on Premium and $10 on Ultimate — the cheapest plan pays four times per credit what the dearest one pays. Anyone topping up regularly on Basic is paying a premium for staying on the cheap tier, and should price the next tier against a month of actual top-ups rather than against the headline gap between the two.
Two smaller things before you pick. Export quality is tiered — 720p on Basic, 1080p on Premium, 4K on Ultimate — so the resolution you need may set your plan before the credits do. And image and audio generation still consume credits on Basic, going unlimited only from Premium up.

video:video.video:title: Niural AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Every tier says Book a demo. The prices are published — which in payroll is genuinely rare and worth crediting — but there is no self-serve sign-up anywhere on the page, so the published figure is the opening of a conversation rather than something you can act on. Expect the real number to arrive by quote, and expect it to depend on the company-size step you selected before you ever saw a price.
The page changes under you, and that is easy to miss. It asks your headcount band first and adjusts the ladder to match, so two people comparing Niural can honestly quote each other different numbers. Note which band you read when you write the figure down.
The platform fee is the part that decides whether this is cheap. US Payroll is $100 a month before anyone is paid, plus $20 a head. At five employees that is $200 a month, or $40 an employee — double the headline rate. At twenty-five it is $600, or $24 each. At a hundred it is $2,100, or $21 each. The per-employee price you are quoted only becomes the price you pay somewhere north of fifty people, and small teams are the ones most likely to read $20 and budget $20.
The naming needs care too. Contractor of Record and Employer of Record are both $299 per employee a month and they are not the same product: the first keeps the worker a contractor while Niural carries the misclassification risk, the second makes Niural the legal employer in 150-plus countries. Buying the wrong one is an expensive mistake that the identical price does nothing to prevent.

video:video.video:title: NordPass Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Teams is sold only as a 10-user pack and Business and Enterprise have a 5-user minimum, so very small teams pay for empty seats. SSO with Entra ID, ADFS or Okta is only on Enterprise. The Free plan does not sync across devices, and personal prices are introductory for the first term, with a higher regular price shown next to them. Prices exclude VAT. We have not used NordPass ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Nouswise Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Their own site does not agree with itself about what this costs, and we have now checked that twice. The pricing page says Essential 19.99$/month and Pro 49.99$/month; the homepage, read the same day, shows a pricing block with $10.00 and $40.00. We put the gap to Nouswise, and on 18 Aug 2026 their partner manager answered that the homepage figures are a counter animation and that a normal browser with JavaScript enabled would show 19.99 and 49.99. We did exactly that check the same day — an ordinary browser, JavaScript on, waiting for the animation to settle — and the homepage still read $10.00 for Essential and $40.00 for Professional. So the gap is real, the vendor's own explanation for it did not hold, and neither page flags the other. Get the number in writing for the tier and the billing period you want before you put a card in, because there is a documented chance of paying double what a landing page just promised you.
The headline claim needs the same care. The homepage says “100% Verifiable AI Answers” and that answers are “solely drawn from the provided sources, reducing any fact fabrication to zero”. That is Nouswise describing Nouswise: nobody independent has tested it and neither have we. Grounding an answer in a curated library genuinely does cut invention, but it does not make retrieval, ranking or summarising error-free, and it cannot make an answer better than the library it came from. If your library is thin, outdated or one-sided, a confident grounded answer is still the wrong answer — with a citation attached. Two other numbers on that page, the 25% of the workweek spent searching and the 2.4 billion hours a year inside the Fortune 500, carry no source on the page at all.
Three smaller things worth knowing. The source ceilings are low for organisational use — 50 documents on Starter, 300 on Essential — and unlimited sources only start at Pro. The per-day limits on reports, flashcards and quizzes carry an asterisk explained only as “Limits are a

video:video.video:title: Oyster Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The two numbers that decide your bill are not on the price card. Oyster holds a refundable deposit per EOR employee: working capital out of your account before anyone is paid. It also takes an FX fee whenever the payment currency differs from the contract currency, which for a genuinely global team is most of the time. Neither has a figure attached anywhere we could find. So the honest position is that $699 is the floor, and the real per-employee cost depends on a deposit and a spread you have to ask for. The contractor product is a different shape and much cheaper at $29, so decide which one you actually need. Misclassifying a contractor as an employee is expensive; misclassifying the other way is what the $699 exists to prevent.

video:video.video:title: PDWare Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is genuine enterprise software with enterprise buying: opaque pricing, demo-first sales and implementation effort — appropriate for portfolio offices planning hundreds of resources, overkill below that. The honest pre-purchase question is organizational: resource-first planning only works if your PMO will actually maintain forecasts; the tool formalizes discipline, it can't create it.

video:video.video:title: Pangram Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The unavoidable honest limit of every AI detector, including accurate ones: it is never infallible. It will occasionally flag genuinely human writing as AI (false positives) and miss some AI text, so it must be used as a signal, never as sole proof for high-stakes calls like academic penalties or hiring. Pangram's pitch is fewer false positives than rivals, which is real progress — but 'fewer' is not 'none'. Pair it with human judgment and the credit meter with your actual volume: the free tier's 2,000 words a day are 20 credits rounded up per check, which in our test meant ten checks of 150 words rather than twenty.

video:video.video:title: Parim Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Unlimited users sounds like the generous part, and it is — until you notice what replaces per-seat pricing: a bill that scales with shifts scheduled. For a staffing agency or an events business, shift volume is the one number that swings hardest month to month, which makes this the least predictable pricing model in the category. Before you commit, ask for the price at your busiest month rather than your average, and ask what happens when you cross a threshold.

video:video.video:title: Pdfdodo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The refund rules contradict each other: the FAQ says no refunds of any kind, the terms promise refunds within 30 days of purchase. The yearly Solo card shows $20 a month beside $200 billed yearly, which cannot both be right, and no plan names its currency. Cancelling means sending an email rather than a button in the app.

video:video.video:title: Planday Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The €25 monthly platform fee on Plus is the line most comparisons miss. At the 10-user minimum, Plus is €49.90 in seats plus €25 flat, so €74.90 against €14.95 for five users on Starter — the jump is not from €2.99 to €4.99, it is roughly five times the bill. That fee also does not scale down, so the smaller your team, the larger a share of it you carry. Work out your real per-head cost at your actual headcount before choosing, and check which side of the line leave management and payroll integrations fall on, because those are the two features that usually force the upgrade.

video:video.video:title: Plansom Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The thing you cannot check is the price. plansom.com publishes no figure, /pricing returns 404, and there is no pricing link in the navigation — the only routes to a number are the signup or a sales conversation. The integration list is no longer the weak spot it once was: Claude, ChatGPT, Slack, Gmail, Outlook, Notion, HubSpot, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Zoom and Fireflies are all named on the homepage, and there is a published Microsoft collaboration behind the Teams work. But it is still the smaller player next to Asana, ClickUp and Motion, and it has repositioned around AI agents that run tasks for you. Agent work is usually metered, so ask what a unit of it costs before you compare anything.

video:video.video:title: Plesk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest notes. Plesk has been raising prices steadily (the 2026 round averaged ~26%), so budget for the renewal trajectory, not today's invoice — it's a recurring theme in the ecosystem since the acquisition era. And the domain caps are the real tier-driver: growing past 10 or 30 domains bumps you up a license, so count your domains including the parked ones before choosing.

video:video.video:title: Prezi Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing table puts PDF export and portable presentations at Plus, not Standard, and our free account's AI editor locked PDF, PowerPoint and SCORM downloads to Plus. The zooming format is polarising: some audiences find it engaging, others find it disorienting.

video:video.video:title: Proton Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Storage is the axis, and the jump from Drive Plus to Unlimited is not really about storage at all: you go from 200 GB to 500 GB, but you also start paying for Mail, Calendar, Pass and VPN whether or not you wanted them. If all you need is encrypted file storage, the bundle is where the money leaks. The other thing to price honestly is the encryption itself — end-to-end encryption is the reason to be here, and it is also why per-gigabyte this costs more than the mainstream drives. That is a fair trade if privacy is the requirement, and a poor one if you just want cheap space.

video:video.video:title: Proton Drive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: End-to-end encryption is the point and the price. Because Proton can't read your files, there's no server-side search inside documents. Previews and third-party integrations are more limited than Google Drive or Dropbox, and losing your credentials without recovery set up means losing data — by design. You trade convenience for the mathematical guarantee that nobody, including Proton, can look inside.

video:video.video:title: Qoyod Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry tier does not do the thing the product is sold on. Qoyod's pitch is surviving Saudi e-invoicing, but Basic covers ZATCA Phase 1 only — Phase 2 is the integration phase, where invoices are cleared with the tax authority in real time, and that starts at Pro. If Phase 2 applies to you, your actual floor is 1,800 SAR and not 1,200. The second thing to price before you sign: Basic is genuinely one user and one location, and every extra seat is 240 SAR a year, which is a fifth of the whole Basic plan per person. A four-person shop on Basic pays 1,200 + 3×240 = 1,920 SAR, more than Pro costs while still sitting on Phase 1. Add a single POS user at 600 SAR and the arithmetic tips further. Work out your seat and location count first, then pick the tier — doing it the other way round is how the add-on line becomes the biggest number on the invoice.

video:video.video:title: QuickBooks UK Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 90% offer is the number to be careful with, because it is the one you will see everywhere and it is not what you will pay. The page says six months, not a year: Sole Trader Plus shows £1 and renews at £10 a month, Plus shows £5.60 and renews at £56. That tenfold step arrives in month seven, on a tool you will by then have your entire bookkeeping inside — which is precisely when switching is hardest. Add 20% VAT on top of every figure, and add payroll separately if you need it. Budget from the list price and treat the discount as a half-year rebate, not as the price.

video:video.video:title: QuillBot Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is deliberately narrow: 125 words per paraphrase and two of the modes. The honest framing is that this is a box of writing utilities -- paraphraser, grammar, plagiarism, AI detection -- rather than somewhere you actually write. General AI chat tools now overlap much of it. And treat the free AI detector as weak: in our test of 1 October 2026 it rated four plainly written machine texts 100% human and only caught a paragraph full of stock chatbot phrases. Note the sticker too: the advertised €8.33 a month assumes you pay for the year, and month-to-month is €19.95, about 2.4 times as much.

video:video.video:title: Recruit CRM Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline seat price is not the whole bill: the features recruiters use daily for outreach run on credits, and LinkedIn messaging alone uses 150 credits per user a month while Pro includes 100. The pricing table says unlimited candidates and contacts, but the help centre sets per-user record limits (10,000 each on Pro). Annual billing is charged upfront and the subscription article rules out refunds for unused time, so a wrong tier choice is expensive to undo.

video:video.video:title: Remote People Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The monthly rates are the cheapest we have on file for this category, and that is worth saying plainly.
