Our Deel dossier has EOR from $599 per employee a month against Remote People’s $199, contractor of record $325 against $199, US PEO $125 against $99 and contractor management $49 against $29. If those hold at your headcount and in your country, the gap is large enough to matter.
Two things stop that from being the whole picture. First, every figure on the page carries a ‘from’ and not one country-level rate is published. EOR pricing moves with statutory employer cost, which varies enormously between, say, Portugal and Brazil, so the number you are quoted for your actual hire is the only one that counts. Ask for it in writing before you compare anything.
Second, and larger: the recruitment services are priced as a share of salary, and that dwarfs the subscription. Global Recruitment at 20% of annual salary on an $80,000 hire is $16,000 due on day one — more than six years of EOR Flex for the same person. Executive Search at 25% is more again. Recruit + EOR at 2% over twelve months is a different animal entirely and is the one worth understanding, because it is the only route where the fee is spread rather than paid up front. Nothing on the pricing page puts these side by side, so it is easy to read the $199 and miss where the money actually goes.
One structural note: EOR Plus needs a minimum of five employees and an annual commitment, so a small team comparing tiers is really only choosing Flex.

video:video.video:title: Replit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The subscription price is fixed; the paid Agent work is not. Everyday building can run in Free Mode at no extra cost, within an allowance that resets every five hours on Core and Pro and a daily cap on Starter, but anything past it is billed by effort, and only Pro's unused credits roll over. Replit asks before each paid request starts and lets you set a budget, so set one before long sessions. Great for learning and prototyping; watch the meter for production work.

video:video.video:title: Rippling Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The published '$8 per employee a month' is real but it's only the floor, it comes with a monthly base fee ($40 on the small-business page), and it's the HR-and-payroll entry — not the price of the platform. Rippling sells HR, IT and Finance as separate, separately-quoted modules, so you can't comparison-shop without a sales call, and a single-module deployment pays platform prices for a point tool. You're buying a system of record; the value only shows up once you consolidate several systems onto it.

video:video.video:title: Runpod Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest math is utilization. On the same card serverless runs roughly 1.7x the pod rate per compute-hour: $4.79 against $2.89 for an H100, $2.72 against $1.59 for an A100 PCIe. That is brilliant for spiky inference and wasteful for steady training, so pick the mode per workload, not per habit. And like all GPU clouds, the meter never sleeps: an idle pod you forgot is the cloud version of the subscription graveyard. Set spend alerts before the first experiment, not after the first invoice.

video:video.video:title: Samsara Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Seven named packages and not one price. The pricing page asks how many vehicles you run and leads to a sales form; the plans page ends every package in Get pricing. The contract side is public and worth reading before the call: under section 13.1 of the Platform Terms, if you do not cancel auto-renewal in writing at least 30 days before the licence ends, Samsara may renew for up to a year or the length of your previous term, whichever is greater. Put that date in your calendar on day one. Licensed hardware is covered for as long as the licence runs; accessories and cables get one year.

video:video.video:title: Sendcloud Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing has layers — a per-label fee on top of the subscription, plus carrier surcharges that can land on invoices weeks later. It's built out-of-the-box, so deep customisation is limited, there's no inventory management (ShipStation has it), and high-volume shippers (€12k+/mo) plus pickup-reliability complaints suggest it's happiest with small-to-mid EU stores.

video:video.video:title: Sentaro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The category claim (AI catches what filters miss) is plausible — Microsoft/Google native filtering misses sophisticated BEC — but any vendor's accuracy percentage is measured on their own test set, not your mail flow. The honest procurement move: run their trial alongside your current filtering, count real catches and false positives for two weeks, and price per mailbox against the incumbents with that data in hand.

video:video.video:title: Shoeboxed Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Its unique trick is the Magic Envelope, where you literally mail a stuffed envelope of paper receipts and humans digitize them. That trick is also the meter to watch: envelope frequency defines the tiers, and heavy paper businesses land in the $179/mo bracket quickly. If your receipts are already digital, cheaper scan-only apps exist; Shoeboxed earns its price precisely when physical paper is the problem.

video:video.video:title: Shopmonkey Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Card processing is part of the product, but the online and in-person payment rates are 'Call for Pricing' on every plan, so you cannot work out the full monthly cost from the page. Inventory, purchase orders and unlimited inspections are not in the $215 Basic plan, a $500 migration fee and $299 card readers come on top, and there is no free trial or self-serve signup, only a demo. We have not used Shopmonkey ourselves.

video:video.video:title: ShortlistIQ Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: No yearly prices are shown although the FAQ mentions yearly plans, and the cards do not name their currency. Basic covers only 20 applicants a month with a single AI assistant. Unused or partly used service is not refunded on early cancellation, and the homepage selling point, that candidates cannot tell the AI from a person, puts the duty to disclose on you.

video:video.video:title: Signable Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Business and Enterprise prices are only 'from' figures and go through sales, and the overage fee for envelopes beyond your allowance is not published. Unused envelopes on a paid plan are lost at the end of the billing period. The API, bulk send and Qualified Electronic Signatures all start on Business, from £100 a month, not on Essentials.

video:video.video:title: TestGorilla Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The Assessments bill is set by credits, and the page does not say how many credits its 'from' prices include. Core starts from $77 a month billed annually or from $287 billed monthly; that gap is far wider than the 25% annual saving the page advertises, so the two floors are different allowances. An AI interview costs 2 credits a candidate and a skills test 1, so the real price depends on how you build each assessment and how many people you invite. Get the credit allowance in writing before you compare it with a per-seat tool.

video:video.video:title: TextExpander Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: On a Mac the operating system already does the basic job free: Apple's built-in Text Replacement syncs static snippets across your Apple devices, though Apple's own documentation notes it is not available in every app. And Espanso covers the power-user case free and open source on Mac, Windows and Linux. On Windows there is no built-in equivalent (contrary to a widely repeated claim, PowerToys has no text-expansion utility), so the case for paying is genuinely stronger there. On mobile, only iPhone and iPad are covered: the vendor's mobile page, read 9 October 2026, offers a keyboard app for those, while Android is still a beta signup. Then add the snippet activity history: nothing at all on the free plan, only 24 hours on the $5 Pro tier, 7 days on Business, and unlimited only on Enterprise. Add the vendor's own note that buyers in VAT/GST countries including the EU, UK and Australia may see an estimated 20% uplift on the listed USD price (read 21 July 2026). For one person with a few dozen fixed snippets, the honest answer is usually don't.

video:video.video:title: Top Echelon Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Almost everything people shop for sits in Professional, not Standard: Smart-TE AI, automations, sequences, inbound email sync and API access are all one tier up, so Standard is a competent but plain ATS. The bigger thing to price honestly is that TE Recruit and TE Network are two separate subscriptions. The network is billed per agency on top of your seats, so "Top Echelon" can mean two bills. And taking the network month-to-month adds a $350 one-time startup fee that annual billing waives.

video:video.video:title: Tresorit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You pay the Swiss-E2EE premium — noticeably above mainstream clouds and above Proton Drive per GB — and the encryption trade-offs are inherent: no server-side content search, more deliberate sharing flows, and credential/recovery discipline is on you. For regulated teams that's exactly the deal; for casual storage it's over-engineering.

video:video.video:title: VideoScribe Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Payments are non-refundable according to the help centre, and a monthly plan must be cancelled at least three business days before the next payment. Lite still watermarks premium images and caps you at 5 downloads of up to 5 minutes a month; AI voiceover starts on Core. Monthly billing costs more than twice the annual rate.

video:video.video:title: WPLP Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The paid platform sells breadth, not a different product: the free WPLP Cookie Consent plugin already includes the cookie banner, the scanner, script blocking, a consent log and Google Consent Mode v2 according to its own listing, so a single site may never need to pay. Three headline features on the pricing page, automatic policy updates, automated data-request processing and the compliance blueprint, are marked coming soon. The legal pages come from a questionnaire and templates, not from a lawyer. It is WordPress only. And the vendor's own numbers do not line up: the pricing page says 20,000+ sites, the cookie plugin's listing 30,000+, and the Legal Pages listing on wordpress.org still has unfilled template placeholders around its install count and around whether premium is a one-time or an annual licence, while the pricing page sells yearly plans. We have not run WPLP ourselves.

video:video.video:title: Wondershare PDFelement Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The prices on the store are a launch discount next to higher list prices, and the yearly plan renews automatically. Every paid plan shows only 50 PDF AI uses and 3 eSign requests in the comparison table. A perpetual licence covers PDFelement 13, not later major versions, and the prices we read are for one platform. We have not used PDFelement ourselves.

video:video.video:title: World Businesses for Sale Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: On the broker plans you pay twice: a listing fee up front AND commission when it sells — 3% on Basic, 2% on Standard, 1% on Premium — on contracts of 6, 9 and 12 months. Only Premium stays live until sold with free renewals, so on the lower tiers a business that has not sold needs a paid renewal, and for a slow sale £1,500 once can beat £749 twice. Every tier says commission is payable only when they introduce the buyer, which is exactly the clause to read in the contract before you sign. If you want no commission at all, the pay-as-you-go plans start at £49 a month, or £147 for six months — far cheaper up front, but those are listings, not broker introductions. As with any marketplace, the fee buys exposure, not a guaranteed sale.

video:video.video:title: Your Company Formations Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The £2.48 headline leaves out the £100 Companies House fee and 20% VAT on the package, and every basket starts with a £5.99 review you have to remove yourself. The address and filing services in the bigger packages renew every year, at £28 to £128 each. And the terms tie refunds to the services ordered and say cancellation may be subject to a minimum contract duration.

video:video.video:title: Zenind Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $0 Basic package covers filing only. A registered agent costs $99 a year on every package, the operating agreement is $99 extra on Basic, and state filing fees always come on top, so the real first-year cost is well above $0. Basic also takes up to 7 days to file. Annual report filing is included only on Premium and only for the first year, then $100 a year plus state fees. Zenind is not a law firm and does not give legal advice. We have not used Zenind ourselves.

video:video.video:title: doola Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Formation is the cheap part; the recurring bookkeeping and tax tiers are where the real cost sits, and state fees are extra on top of doola's price. Convenient especially for non-US founders, but a local accountant may be cheaper once you're established.
